unit.can_do_en: accept an invitation and thank the host.

brief.situation_en: Ahmed invites Maria to his birthday.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text_kirja: Minä pidän syntymäpäiväjuhlat lauantaina. Tulisitko sinä?
lines.gloss_en: I'm having a birthday party on Saturday. Would you come?

judge.reason: Only register differences (synttärit/syntymäpäiväjuhlat, mä/minä, sä/sinä, dropped -ko); same meaning.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Thanks for the invitation! I'd love to come.

judge.reason: Kiitti is colloquial for kiitos; rest identical.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text_puhe: Hienoo! Se alkaa kuudelta mun luona.
lines.text_kirja: Hienoa! Se alkaa kuudelta minun luonani.
lines.gloss_en: Great! It starts at six at my place.

judge.reason: Hienoo/hienoa and mun luona/minun luonani are register variants; same time and place.
Voinks mä is spoken for voinko minä; same question.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text_puhe: Ei tarvii. Mut jos haluut, jälkkäri ois kiva.
lines.text_kirja: Ei tarvitse. Mutta jos haluat, jälkiruoka olisi kiva.
lines.gloss_en: No need. But if you want, a dessert would be nice.

judge.reason: Ei tarvii/tarvitse, mut/mutta, haluut/haluat, jälkkäri/jälkiruoka, ois/olisi are all register variants.
Mä/minä only; same statement about chocolate balls.
Ne on is spoken for ne ovat; same question.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Brazilian chocolate balls. You'll love them!

judge.reason: Brasilialaisii/brasilialaisia and sä/sinä are register variants; same content.

forms.why_en: Means 'I'. Spoken Finnish often says 'mä'.

forms.lemma_meaning_en: to have to, to like, to hold
forms.why_en: Pitää changes to pidä- and takes -n for 'I': pidän. Pitää juhlat means 'to have a party'.
Books write syntymäpäiväjuhlat and speech says synttärit. Both end in -t, as a party is several celebrations.

forms.form_name_en: conditional present tense, 2nd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: -isi- means 'would' and -t goes with sinä. Speech says tulisitsä instead of the -ko question.
Means 'you' (one person). Spoken: 'sä'.
Thank you, said by the customer; in casual speech it becomes kiitti.
Thanking takes -sta: kutsu becomes kutsusta, 'for the invitation'.
tulla means to come. -isi- means 'would' and -n goes with minä: tulisin.

forms.form_name_en: adessive singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: A fixed word meaning 'gladly'. It comes from mieli, 'mind', with -ni for 'my'.
Exclamations like this take -a: hieno becomes hienoa. Speech turns -oa into -oo.
'It.' Nominative singular, referring back to the price.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Clock times take -lta: kuusi becomes kuudelta, 'at six'.
Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.

forms.form_name_en: adverb, with the possessive ending for my
present tense, 1st person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Voin, I can, with -ko to ask. Speech says -ks: voinks.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The partitive singular of jokin 'something': jotain. People say it the same way.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. Speech says it the same way.
Means 'but'. It links two ideas: from Tampere, but home is in Helsinki.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Adds -t for 'you': haluta becomes haluat. Speech says haluut.
This is the dictionary form. Speech says jälkkäri for jälkiruoka.
The conditional adds -isi for 'would': olla becomes olisi. Speech shortens olisi to ois.
Means 'nice'; 'Kiva tavata' = 'Nice to meet you'.
Tehdä 'to do' becomes tee- and adds -n for 'I': teen. People say it the same way.
An open number of things takes -ja: suklaapallo becomes suklaapalloja.
The partitive of mikä, what. Mitä saa olla? means What can I get you?
Ne means they, for things. Speech also uses it for people.
Books write ovat for 'they are'. Speech uses on for one thing or many.
Describing an open number of things takes -ia: brasilialainen becomes brasilialaisia. Speech says -ii.
Tykätä changes to tykkää- and takes -t for 'you': tykkäät.
